full_title: PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. ARISTON PATERNO, JR. Y SALES, ACCUSED-APPELLANT.
subject: Criminal Law
syllabus_topic: III. The Revised Penal Code – Book Two > E. Title V – Crimes Relative to Opium and Other Prohibited Drugs > 1. Repealed. See instead Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002 (RA 9165, Art. II, as amended by RA 10640; See also AM 18-03-16-SC)
topics: Penalty for illegal possession of 5 to less than 10 grams of shabu (RA 9165, Sec. 11[2])
Life imprisonment as maximum only when Sec. 13 circumstances are present
Indeterminate Sentence Law applied to a range penalty under a special law
Chain of custody: unruly accused and commotion do not justify marking and inventory at the police station

doctrine:
**While the imposable penalty for illegal possession of five grams or more but less than 10 grams of shabu under Section 11(2) of RA 9165 is 20 years and one day to life imprisonment, the maximum of life imprisonment may be imposed only when the circumstances in Section 13 are present**, i.e., the accused was found "possessing any dangerous drug during a party, or at a social gathering or meeting, or in the proximate company of at least [two] persons." Otherwise, a maximum term **below** life imprisonment must be imposed so the accused can avail of the Indeterminate Sentence Law, which by its Section 2 does not apply to persons convicted of offenses punished with life imprisonment. The Court followed *People v. Pis-an* and the reasoning in then Justice Peralta's concurring opinion in *People v. Obias*, which it quoted, and imposed 20 years and one day, as minimum, to 30 years, as maximum, where there was neither allegation nor proof of a Section 13 circumstance.

On chain of custody (reiterated): for offenses committed while RA 10640 was in effect, the inventory need only be witnessed by the accused or his representative or counsel, an elected public official, and a representative of the National Prosecution Service **or** the media; a DOJ representative is not required. Following *People v. Casa*, marking, inventory and photographing must be done at the place of seizure unless the safety of the officers, the witnesses or the items is threatened by immediate or extreme danger. **That the accused became unruly and his sister and friends caused a commotion is not a justifiable ground to do the marking and inventory at the police station**; the unjustified deviation renders the seizure and custody void, compromises the integrity of the drugs, and warrants acquittal. Drugs found in a later search at the police station, immediately marked and inventoried there before the required witnesses, and traced through an unbroken chain of custody, may still support a conviction for possession.
facts:
Ariston Paterno, Jr. was charged in Legazpi City with illegal sale of dangerous drugs (Criminal Case No. 14279), for selling on or about February 1, 2015 one sachet containing 4.608 grams of shabu for PHP 12,000.00, and with illegal possession (Criminal Case No. 14280), for possessing two sachets marked NBG-2 (0.470 gram) and NBG-3 (4.732 grams) of shabu with a gross weight of 5.202 grams. He pleaded not guilty.

According to the prosecution, a confidential informant told PO2 Noel Grutas around 6:00 p.m. of February 1, 2015 that drug users and pushers were going to Paterno's house. A buy-bust was arranged with PO2 Grutas as poseur-buyer, using two marked PHP 500.00 bills and 11 pieces of PHP 1,000.00 boodle money. Around 10:30 p.m., Paterno handed PO2 Grutas a sachet from his shoulder bag in exchange for the money, and the team arrested him. While being apprised of his rights, Paterno became unruly and shouted, calling the neighbors' attention, so the officers brought him, the sachet and his bag to the police station. There, in the presence of barangay representatives and a media representative, PO2 Grutas inspected the bag and recovered the buy-bust money and two more sachets. The items were marked and inventoried at the station, the inventory was signed by the witnesses, and the sachets tested positive for methamphetamine hydrochloride.

Paterno claimed a frame-up: men in civilian clothes barged into his boarding house, mauled him, and found nothing on him at the scene, and drugs were "found" only after he was frisked several times at the station.

The RTC convicted him of both charges, imposing life imprisonment and a PHP 500,000.00 fine for the sale, and 20 years and one day to life imprisonment and a PHP 400,000.00 fine for the possession. The CA affirmed in toto, holding that marking at the nearest police station in the presence of the accused complied with the chain of custody rule. Paterno appealed, arguing that the items were not marked at the place of arrest and that no DOJ representative witnessed the inventory.
issues: Whether the absence of a DOJ representative at the inventory violated Section 21 of RA 9165, as amended.
Whether the failure to mark and inventory the sachet subject of the sale at the place of arrest, for the reasons given, warrants Paterno's acquittal of illegal sale.
Whether Paterno's conviction for illegal possession should be upheld.
Whether the penalty of 20 years and one day to life imprisonment for illegal possession was proper.
ruling:
**1. No.** The crime was committed while RA 10640 was in effect, which requires only "the accused or the person/s from whom such items were confiscated and/or seized, or his/her representative or counsel, with an elected public official and a representative of the National Prosecution Service or the media" to witness the inventory. Barangay officials and a media representative witnessed it, so the witness requirement was met.

**2. Yes, Paterno must be acquitted of illegal sale.** The prosecution justified marking the sold sachet at the police station because Paterno became unruly and his sister and friends caused a commotion, forcing the officers to leave for security reasons. In *People v. Casa*, the Court En Banc collected cases rejecting similar excuses: a crowd of 200 people (*Dumanjug*) and a crowd that was "getting bigger" (*Salenga*). Under *Lim*, inventory and photographing at the nearest police station are excused only when the safety of the officers, witnesses or items is threatened by immediate or extreme danger, such as retaliatory action by those with the resources and capability to mount a counter-assault. **"The buy-bust team's excuses that accused-appellant became unruly and that his sister and friends caused a commotion at the place of arrest were not justifiable grounds to conduct the marking and inventory at the police station."** The seizure and custody of the sold sachet were rendered void and its integrity compromised.

**3. Yes.** The two other sachets were recovered from Paterno at the police station and immediately marked and inventoried there in the presence of the mandatory witnesses. The prosecution established their movement and custody from seizure until turnover to the trial court, so their integrity and evidentiary value remained intact.

**4. No.** Section 11(2) of RA 9165 prescribes 20 years and one day to life imprisonment, but under Section 13, the maximum penalties of Section 11 apply to one found possessing drugs during a party, at a social gathering or meeting, or in the proximate company of at least two persons. The Court quoted then Justice Peralta's concurring opinion in *People v. Obias*: although the Revised Penal Code rules on graduation do not apply to this special law, the Indeterminate Sentence Law applies when the penalty is a range; an indeterminate sentence with life imprisonment as the maximum would deny parole, and Section 2 of the ISL excludes persons convicted of offenses punished with life imprisonment. "It is only when the illegal possession under Section 11 . . . is committed in the presence of two or more persons or in a social gathering that the maximum penalty of life imprisonment may be imposed." Following *People v. Pis-an*, and **with neither allegation nor proof of a Section 13 circumstance, the sentence was modified to 20 years and one day, as minimum, to 30 years, as maximum.**
disposition: Appeal PARTIALLY GRANTED; the CA Decision of November 19, 2020 in CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 12805 was AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION. In Criminal Case No. 14279, Paterno was ACQUITTED of illegal sale of dangerous drugs on reasonable doubt, with entry of judgment to issue immediately. In Criminal Case No. 14280, he was found GUILTY of illegal possession of dangerous drugs and sentenced to an indeterminate penalty of 20 years and one day, as minimum, to 30 years, as maximum, and a fine of PHP 400,000.00. Copies were ordered furnished to the Chief of the PNP and the Director General of the PDEA, and the RTC was directed to turn over the sachets to the Dangerous Drugs Board for destruction.

bar_questions.q: During the lawful search of his house, police officers found Ramon alone in his bedroom with a sachet containing 6.2 grams of shabu. He was charged with illegal possession of dangerous drugs under Section 11 of RA 9165. The Information alleged no other circumstance, and the evidence showed that no one else was with Ramon. After trial, the court convicted him and sentenced him to an indeterminate penalty with life imprisonment as the maximum. Is life imprisonment a proper maximum term?

alac.answer: No. Life imprisonment may not be the maximum term because no Section 13 circumstance was alleged or proven.
alac.legal_basis: Section 11(2) of RA 9165 punishes possession of five grams or more but less than 10 grams of shabu with 20 years and one day to life imprisonment. The maximum of life imprisonment may be imposed only when the circumstances in Section 13 are present: possession during a party, at a social gathering or meeting, or in the proximate company of at least two persons. Otherwise, the maximum term must be below life imprisonment so that the accused may avail of the Indeterminate Sentence Law, which under its Section 2 does not apply to persons convicted of offenses punished with life imprisonment. (People v. Paterno, G.R. No. 256964, August 13, 2025, following People v. Pis-an)
alac.application: Ramon possessed 6.2 grams of shabu, so Section 11(2) applies. But he was alone in his bedroom, and the Information alleged no party, gathering or company of at least two persons. Without a Section 13 circumstance, imposing life imprisonment as the maximum would deny him the benefits of the Indeterminate Sentence Law, such as parole. The court should impose an indeterminate sentence whose maximum is below life imprisonment, as the Court did in Paterno.
alac.conclusion: The sentence is erroneous; the maximum term must be below life imprisonment.

bar_questions.q: Same facts as in the previous question, except that the police found Ramon holding the sachet of 6.2 grams of shabu during a drinking session in his house with four friends. The Information alleged, and the prosecution proved, that he possessed the drugs at a social gathering and in the proximate company of at least two persons. May the court impose life imprisonment, and does the Indeterminate Sentence Law apply?

alac.answer: Yes, the court may impose life imprisonment, and the Indeterminate Sentence Law does not apply.
alac.legal_basis: Under Section 13 of RA 9165, any person found possessing any dangerous drug during a party, or at a social gathering or meeting, or in the proximate company of at least two persons, shall suffer the maximum penalties provided for in Section 11, regardless of the quantity and purity of the drugs. It is only when the possession is committed in these circumstances that the maximum penalty of life imprisonment may be imposed, and only then is the Indeterminate Sentence Law no longer applicable, since Section 2 of that law excludes persons convicted of offenses punished with life imprisonment. (People v. Paterno, G.R. No. 256964, August 13, 2025)
alac.application: Unlike in Paterno, where there was neither allegation nor proof of a Section 13 circumstance, here the Information alleged and the evidence proved that Ramon possessed the shabu at a drinking session with four friends. Section 13 therefore requires the maximum penalty under Section 11(2), which is life imprisonment. Because the penalty imposed is life imprisonment, the Indeterminate Sentence Law cannot apply.
alac.conclusion: Ramon may be sentenced to life imprisonment, and he cannot avail of the Indeterminate Sentence Law.

bar_questions.q: In 2016, police officers arrested Ben right after he sold a sachet of shabu to a poseur-buyer. Ben resisted and shouted, and his relatives and neighbors gathered and argued with the officers. Citing the commotion, the officers brought Ben and the sachet to the police station, where they marked and inventoried the sachet in the presence of a barangay kagawad and a media representative. Ben, charged with illegal sale, argues that (a) the inventory is invalid because no DOJ representative was present, and (b) the officers had no valid reason to do the marking and inventory at the station. Rule on each argument.

alac.answer: (a) The first argument fails; no DOJ representative was required. (b) The second argument is correct; Ben should be acquitted of illegal sale.
alac.legal_basis: Under Section 21 of RA 9165, as amended by RA 10640, the inventory must be witnessed by the accused or his representative or counsel, an elected public official, and a representative of the National Prosecution Service or the media. Marking, inventory and photographing must be done at the place of seizure unless the safety of the officers, witnesses or items is threatened by immediate or extreme danger, such as retaliatory action by those with the resources to mount a counter-assault (People v. Casa). An accused becoming unruly and relatives or friends causing a commotion are not justifiable grounds to move the marking and inventory to the police station; the unjustified deviation renders the seizure and custody void and compromises the integrity of the drugs. (People v. Paterno, G.R. No. 256964, August 13, 2025)
alac.application: (a) The sale happened in 2016, after RA 10640 took effect, so the presence of an elected official (the barangay kagawad) and a media representative satisfied the witness requirement. (b) But the only reason for leaving the scene was Ben's resistance and a crowd of relatives and neighbors arguing with the officers. That is not the immediate or extreme danger that excuses marking and inventory away from the place of seizure. The deviation is unjustified, so the integrity and evidentiary value of the sachet are compromised.
alac.conclusion: The witness requirement was met, but the unjustified marking and inventory at the police station creates reasonable doubt, so Ben should be acquitted of illegal sale.

notes: The Decision's opening paragraph cites "Republic Act No. 9615," an evident typographical error for RA 9165. In the body, the sale case is referred to as "Criminal Case No. 14729" and the possession case as "Criminal Case No. 14780"; the Informations and the fallo use Nos. 14279 and 14280. The possession Information alleges "on or about February 2, 2015," while the narrated facts place the arrest on February 1, 2015 and the sachets bear the marking "02-01-15." The rule on the maximum term follows People v. Pis-an and the reasoning of Justice Peralta's concurring opinion in People v. Obias, which the main opinion quoted and adopted. Describing Pis-an, the Decision says the maximum imposable penalty "should be below life imprisonment which is pegged at 40 years and one day"; the phrase is ambiguous and is not relied on in this digest. The Court did not separately discuss the prayer to acquit on the ground of an invalid buy-bust operation beyond the chain of custody issues.
